[LocalDateTime].\n *\n * This class represents dates without a reference to a particular time zone.\n * As such, these objects may denote different time intervals in different time zones: for someone in Berlin,\n * `2020-08-30` started and ended at different moments from those for someone in Tokyo.\n *\n * The arithmetic on [LocalDate] values is defined independently of the time zone (so `2020-08-30` plus one day\n * is `2020-08-31` everywhere): see various [LocalDate.plus] and [LocalDate.minus] functions, as well\n * as [LocalDate.periodUntil] and various other [*until][LocalDate.daysUntil] functions.\n *\n * ### Arithmetic operations\n *\n * Operations with [DateTimeUnit.DateBased] and [DatePeriod] are provided for [LocalDate]:\n * - [LocalDate.plus] and [LocalDate.minus] allow expressing concepts like \"two months later\".\n * - [LocalDate.until] and its shortcuts [LocalDate.daysUntil], [LocalDate.monthsUntil], and [LocalDate.yearsUntil]\n *   can be used to find the number of days, months, or years between two dates.\n * - [LocalDate.periodUntil] (and [LocalDate.minus] that accepts a [LocalDate])\n *   can be used to find the [DatePeriod] between two dates.\n *\n * ### Platform specifics\n *\n * The range of supported years is platform-dependent, but at least is enough to represent dates of all instants between\n * [Instant.DISTANT_PAST] and [Instant.DISTANT_FUTURE].\n *\n * On the JVM,\n * there are `LocalDate.toJavaLocalDate()` and `java.time.LocalDate.toKotlinLocalDate()`\n * extension functions to convert between `kotlinx.datetime` and `java.time` objects used for the same purpose.\n * Similarly, on the Darwin platforms, there is a `LocalDate.toNSDateComponents()` extension function.\n *\n * ### Construction, serialization, and deserialization\n *\n * [LocalDate] can be constructed directly from its components using the constructor.\n * See sample 1.\n *\n * [fromEpochDays] can be used to obtain a [LocalDate] from the number of days since the epoch day `1970-01-01`;\n * [toEpochDays] is the inverse operation.\n * See sample 2.\n *\n * [parse] and [toString] methods can be used to obtain a [LocalDate] from and convert it to a string in the\n * ISO 8601 extended format.\n * See sample 3.\n *\n * [parse] and [LocalDate.format] both support custom formats created with [Format] or defined in [Formats].\n * See sample 4.\n *\n * Additionally, there are several `kotlinx-serialization` serializers for [LocalDate]:\n * - [LocalDateIso8601Serializer] for the ISO 8601 extended format.\n * - [LocalDateComponentSerializer] for an object with components.\n *\n * @sample kotlinx.datetime.test.samples.LocalDateSamples.constructorFunctionMonthNumber\n * @sample kotlinx.datetime.test.samples.LocalDateSamples.fromAndToEpochDays\n * @sample kotlinx.datetime.test.samples.LocalDateSamples.simpleParsingAndFormatting\n * @sample kotlinx.datetime.test.samples.LocalDateSamples.customFormat\n */\n@Serializable(with = fromEpochDays(epochDays: Int): LocalDate\n\n        /**\n         * Creates a new format for parsing and formatting [LocalDate] values.\n         *\n         * Only parsing and formatting of the other.\n        if (Instant.MAX.epochSeconds > Long.MAX_VALUE / 1000) {\n            /* Any number of milliseconds in Long is representable as an Instant */\n            for (instant in {"path":"core/common/src/format/DateTimeComponents.kt","prefix":"/*\n * Copyright 2019-2023 JetBrains s.r.o. and contributors.\n * Use of this source code is governed by the Apache 2.0 License that can be found in the LICENSE.txt file.\n */\n\npackage kotlinx.datetime.format\n\nimport kotlinx.datetime.*\nimport kotlinx.datetime.DayOfWeek\nimport kotlinx.datetime.internal.*\nimport kotlinx.datetime.internal.format.*\nimport kotlinx.datetime.internal.format.parser.Copyable\nimport kotlinx.datetime.internal.safeMultiply\nimport kotlin.reflect.*\n\n/**\n * A collection of datetime fields used specifically for parsing and formatting.\n *\n * Its main purpose is to support complex datetime formats that don't correspond to any of the standard\n * entities in the library. For example, a format that includes only the month and the day of the month but not the\n * year cannot be represented and parsed as a [LocalDate], but it is valid for a [DateTimeComponents].\n * See sample 1.\n *\n * Another purpose is to support parsing and formatting data with out-of-bounds values. For example, parsing\n * `23:59:60` as a [LocalTime] is not possible, but it is possible to parse it as a [DateTimeComponents], adjust the value by\n * setting [second] to `59`, and then convert it to a [LocalTime] via [toLocalTime].\n * See sample 2.\n *\n * Because this class has limited applications, constructing it directly is not possible.\n * For formatting, use the [format] overload that accepts a lambda with a [DateTimeComponents] receiver.\n * See sample 3.\n *\n * Accessing the fields of this class is not thread-safe.\n * Make sure to apply proper synchronization if you are using a single instance from multiple threads.\n *\n * @sample kotlinx.datetime.test.samples.format.DateTimeComponentsSamples.parsingComplexInput\n * @sample kotlinx.datetime.test.samples.format.DateTimeComponentsSamples.parsingInvalidInput\n * @sample kotlinx.datetime.test.samples.format.DateTimeComponentsSamples.simpleFormatting\n */\npublic class kotlinx.datetime.test.samples.format.DateTimeComponentsSamples.customFormat\n         */\n        @Suppress(\"FunctionName\")\n        public fun Format(block: DateTimeFormatBuilder.WithDateTimeComponents.() -> Unit): DateTimeFormat<DateTimeComponents> {\n            val builder = DateTimeComponentsFormat.Builder(AppendableFormatStructure())\n            block(builder)\n            return DateTimeComponentsFormat(builder.build())\n        }\n    }\n\n    /**\n     * A collection of formats for parsing and formatting [DateTimeComponents] values.\n public object Formats {\n\n        /**\n         * ISO 8601 extended format for dates and times with UTC offset.\n         *\n         * The format uses the [UtcOffset.Formats.ISO] format to specify the time zone offset, except that\n         * specifying the minutes of the offset is optional during parsing (so offsets like `+03` are also allowed).\n         *\n         * This format differs from [LocalTime.Formats.ISO] in its time part in that\n         * specifying the seconds is *not* optional.\n         *\n         * Examples of instants in the ISO 8601 format:\n         * - `2020-08-30T18:43:00Z`\n         * - `2020-08-30T18:43:00.50Z`\n         * - `2020-08-30T18:43:00.123456789Z`\n         * - `2020-08-30T18:40:00+03:00`\n         * - `2020-08-30T18:40:00+03:30:20`\n         * * `2020-01-01T23:59:59.123456789+01`\n         * * `+12020-01-31T23:59:59Z`\n         *\n         * This format uses the local date, local time, and UTC offset fields of DateTimeComponents.Formats.ISO_DATE_TIME_OFFSET.parse(\"2020-08-30T18:43:00.123456789+03:00\")\n         * val instant = components.toInstantUsingOffset() // 2020-08-30T15:43:00.123456789Z\n         * val localDateTime = components.toLocalDateTime() // 2020-08-30T18:43:00.123456789\n         * val offset = components.toUtcOffset() // UtcOffset(hours = 3)\n         * ```\n         *\n         * @sample kotlinx.datetime.test.samples.format.DateTimeComponentsSamples.Formats.iso\n         */\n        public val ISO_DATE_TIME_OFFSET: DateTimeFormat<DateTimeComponents> = Format {\n            date(ISO_DATE)\n            alternativeParsing({\n                char('t')\n            }) {\n                char('T')\n            }\n            hour()\n            char(':')\n            minute()\n            char(':')\n            second()\n            optional {\n                char('.')\n                secondFraction(1, 9)\n            }\n            alternativeParsing({\n                offsetHours()\n            }) {\n                offset(UtcOffset.Formats.ISO)\n            }\n        }\n\n        /**\n         * RFC 1123 format for dates and times with UTC offset.\n In particular, resetting the\n    system timezone also resets the default timezone ([NSTimeZone default]) if\n    it's the same as the cached system timezone:\n\n        NSTimeZone.defaultTimeZone = [NSTimeZone\n            timeZoneWithName: [[NSTimeZone systemTimeZone] name]];\n        NSLog(@\"%@\", NSTimeZone.defaultTimeZone.name);\n        NSLog(@\"Change the system time zone, then press Enter\");\n        getchar();\n        [NSTimeZone resetSystemTimeZone];\n        NSLog(@\"%@\", NSTimeZone.defaultTimeZone.name); // will also change\n\n    This is a fairly marginal problem:\n        * It is only a problem when the developer deliberately sets the default\n          timezone to the region that just happens to be the one that the user\n          is in, and then the user moves to another region, and the app also\n          uses the system timezone.\n        * Since iOS 11, the significance of the default timezone has been\n          de-emphasized. In particular, it is not included in the API for\n          Swift: https://forums.swift.org/t/autoupdating-type-properties/4608/4\n\n    Another possible solution could involve using [NSTimeZone localTimeZone].\n    This is documented to reflect the current, uncached system timezone on\n    iOS 11 and later:\n    https://developer.apple.com/documentation/foundation/nstimezone/1387209-localtime","middle":"zone\n    However:\n        * Before iOS 11, this was the same as the default timezone and did not\n          reflect the system timezone.\n        * Worse, on a Mac (10.15.5), I failed to get it to work as documented.\n              NSLog(@\"%@\", NSTimeZone.localTimeZone.name);\n              NSLog(@\"Change the system time zone, then press Enter\");\n              getchar();\n              // [NSTimeZone resetSystemTimeZone]; // uncomment to make it work\n              NSLog(@\"%@\", NSTimeZone.localTimeZone.name);\n          The printed strings are the same even if I wait for good 10 minutes\n          before pressing Enter, unless the line with \"reset\" is uncommented--\n          then the timezone is updated, as it should be. So, for some reason,\n          NSTimeZone.localTimeZone, too, is cached.\n          With no iOS device to test this on, it doesn't seem worth the effort\n          to avoid just resetting the system timezone due to one edge case\n          that's hard to avoid.\n    */\n    NSTimeZone.resetSystemTimeZone()\n    return NSTimeZone.systemTimeZone.name to null\n","suffix":"}\n","code-engine":{"type":"TOKEN_MIDDLE","language":"Kotlin","ce-version":"0.3.119"}}

days = -16, hours = 5).toString() == \"P1Y2M-16DT5H\")\n        check(DateTimePeriod(months = -2, days = -16, hours = -5).toString() == \"-P2M16DT5H\")\n    }\n\n    @Test\n    fun parsing() {\n {"path":"core/common/src/LocalDateTime.kt","prefix":"/*\n * Copyright 2019-2022 JetBrains s.r.o. and contributors.\n * Use of this source code is governed by the Apache 2.0 License that can be found in the LICENSE.txt file.\n */\n\npackage kotlinx.datetime\n\nimport kotlinx.datetime.format.*\nimport kotlinx.datetime.serializers.LocalDateTimeIso8601Serializer\nimport kotlinx.datetime.serializers.LocalDateTimeComponentSerializer\nimport kotlinx.serialization.Serializable\n\n/**\n * The representation of a specific civil date and time without a reference to a particular time zone.\n *\n * This class does not describe specific *moments in time*. For that, use [Instant] values instead.\n * Instead, you can think of its instances as clock readings, which can be observed in a particular time zone.\n * For example, `2020-08-30T18:43` is not a *moment in time* since someone in Berlin and Tokyo would witness\n * this on their clocks at different times, but it is a [LocalDateTime].\n *\n * The main purpose of this class is to provide human-readable representations of [Instant] values, to transfer them\n * as data, or to define future planned events that will have the same local datetime even if the time zone rules\n * change.\n * In all other cases, when a specific time zone is known, it is recommended to use [Instant] instead.\n *\n * ### Arithmetic operations\n *\n * The arithmetic on [LocalDateTime] values is not provided since it may give misleading results\n * without accounting for time zone transitions.\n *\n * For example, in Berlin, naively adding one day to `2021-03-27T02:16:20` without accounting for the time zone would\n * result in `2021-03-28T02:16:20`.\n * However, the resulting local datetime cannot be observed in that time zone\n * because the clocks moved forward from `02:00` to `03:00` on that day.\n * This is known as a \"time gap\" or a \"spring forward\" transition.\n *\n * Similarly, the local datetime `2021-10-31T02:16:20` is ambiguous,\n * because the clocks moved back from `03:00` to `02:00`.\n * This is known as a \"time overlap\" or a \"fall back\" transition.\n *\n * For these reasons, using [LocalDateTime] as an input to arithmetic operations is discouraged.\n *\n * When only the date component is needed, without the time, use [LocalDate] instead.\n * It provides well-defined date arithmetic.\n *\n * If the time component must be taken into account, [LocalDateTime]\n * should be converted to [Instant] using a specific time zone, and the arithmetic on [Instant] should be used.\n *\n * ```\n * val timeZone = TimeZone.of(\"Europe/Berlin\")\n * val localDateTime = LocalDateTime(2021, 3, 27, 2, 16, 20)\n * val instant = localDateTime.toInstant(timeZone)\n *\n * val instantOneDayLater = instant.plus(1, DateTimeUnit.DAY, timeZone)\n * val localDateTimeOneDayLater = instantOneDayLater.toLocalDateTime(timeZone)\n * // 2021-03-28T03:16:20, as 02:16:20 that day is in a time gap\n *\n * val instantTwoDaysLater = instant.plus(2, DateTimeUnit.DAY, timeZone)\n * val localDateTimeTwoDaysLater = instantTwoDaysLater.toLocalDateTime(timeZone)\n * // 2021-03-29T02:16:20\n * ```\n *\n * ### Platform specifics\n *\n * The range of supported years is platform-dependent, but at least is enough to represent dates of all instants between\n * [Instant.DISTANT_PAST] and [Instant.DISTANT_FUTURE].\n *\n * On the JVM, there are `LocalDateTime.toJavaLocalDateTime()` and `java.tim","middle":"e.LocalDateTime.toKotlinLocalDateTime()`\n * extension functions to convert between `kotlinx.datetime` and `java.time` objects used for the same purpose.\n * Similarly, on the Darwin platforms, there is a `LocalDateTime.toNSDateComponents()` extension function.\n *\n * ### Construction, serialization, and deserialization\n *\n * **Pitfall**: since [LocalDateTime] is always constructed without specifying the time zone, it cannot validate\n * whether the given date and time components are valid in the implied time zone.\n * For example, `2021-03-28T02:16:20` is invalid in Berlin, as it falls into a time gap, but nothing prevents one\n * from constructing such a [LocalDateTime].\n * Before using a [LocalDateTime] constructed using any API,\n * please ensure that the result is valid in the implied time zone.\n * The recommended pattern is to convert a [LocalDateTime] to [Instant] as soon as possible (see\n * [LocalDateTime.toInstant]) and work with [Instant] values instead.\n *\n * [LocalDateTime] can be constructed directly from its components, [LocalDate] and [LocalTime], using the constructor.\n * See sample 1.\n *\n * Some additional constructors that directly accept the values from date and time fields are provided for convenience.\n * See sample 2.\n *\n * [parse] and [toString] methods can be used to obtain a [LocalDateTime] from and convert it to a string in the\n * ISO 8601 extended format (for example, `2023-01-02T22:35:01`).\n * See sample 3.\n *\n * [parse] and [LocalDateTime.format] both support custom formats created with [Format] or defined in [Formats].\n * See sample 4.\n *\n * Additionally, there are several `kotlinx-serialization` serializers for [LocalDateTime]:\n * - [LocalDateTimeIso8601Serializer] for the ISO 8601 extended format.\n * - [LocalDateTimeComponentSerializer] for an object with components.\n *\n * @see LocalDate for only the date part of the datetime value.\n * @see LocalTime for only the time part of the datetime value.\n * @see Instant for the representation of a specific moment in time independent of a time zone.\n * @sample kotlinx.datetime.test.samples.LocalDateTimeSamples.fromDateAndTime\n * @sample kotlinx.datetime.test.samples.LocalDateTimeSamples.alternativeConstruction\n * @sample kotlinx.datetime.test.samples.LocalDateTimeSamples.simpleParsingAndFormatting\n * @sample {"path":"core/common/src/Instant.kt","prefix":"/*\n * Copyright 2019-2020 JetBrains s.r.o.\n * Use of this source code is governed by the Apache 2.0 License that can be found in the LICENSE.txt file.\n */\n\npackage kotlinx.datetime\n\nimport kotlinx.datetime.format.*\nimport kotlinx.datetime.internal.*\nimport kotlinx.datetime.serializers.InstantIso8601Serializer\nimport kotlinx.datetime.serializers.InstantComponentSerializer\nimport kotlinx.serialization.Serializable\nimport kotlin.time.*\n\n/**\n * A moment in time.\n *\n * A point in time must be uniquely identified in a way that is independent of a time zone.\n * For example, `1970-01-01, 00:00:00` does not represent a moment in time since this would happen at different times\n * in different time zones: someone in Tokyo would think it is already `1970-01-01` several hours earlier than someone in\n * Berlin would. To represent such entities, use [LocalDateTime].\n * In contrast, \"the moment the clocks in London first showed 00:00 on Jan 1, 2000\" is a specific moment\n * in time, as is \"1970-01-01, 00:00:00 UTC+0\", so it can be represented as an [Instant].\n *\n * `Instant` uses the UTC-SLS (smeared leap second) time scale. This time scale doesn't contain instants\n * corresponding to leap seconds, but instead \"smears\" positive and negative leap seconds among the last 1000 seconds\n * of the day when a leap second happens.\n *\n * ### Obtaining the current moment\n *\n * The [Clock] interface is the primary way to obtain the current moment:\n *\n * ```\n * val clock: Clock = Clock.System\n * val instant = clock.now()\n * ```\n *\n * The [Clock.System] implementation uses the platform-specific system clock to obtain the current moment.\n * Note that this clock is not guaranteed to be monotonic, and the user or the system may adjust it at any time,\n * so it should not be used for measuring time intervals.\n * For that, consider using [TimeSource.Monotonic] and [TimeMark] instead of [Clock.System] and [Instant].\n *\n * ### Obtaining human-readable representations\n *\n * #### Date and time\n *\n * [Instant] is essentially the number of seconds and nanoseconds since a designated moment in time,\n * stored as something like `1709898983.123456789`.\n * [Instant] does not contain information about the day or time, as this depends on the time zone.\n * To work with this information for a specific time zone, obtain a [LocalDateTime] using [Instant.toLocalDateTime]:\n *\n * ```\n * val instant = Instant.fromEpochSeconds(1709898983, 123456789)\n * instant.toLocalDateTime(TimeZone.of(\"Europe/Berlin\")) // 2024-03-08T12:56:23.123456789\n * instant.toLocalDateTime(TimeZone.UTC) // 2024-03-08T11:56:23.123456789\n * ```\n *\n * For values very far in the past or the future, this conversion may fail.\n * The specific range of values that can be converted to [LocalDateTime] is platform-specific, but at least\n * [DISTANT_PAST], [DISTANT_FUTURE], and all values between them can be converted to [LocalDateTime].\n *\n * #### Date or time separately\n *\n * To obtain a [LocalDate] or [LocalTime], first, obtain a [LocalDateTime], and then use its [LocalDateTime.date]\n * and [LocalDateTime.time] properties:\n *\n * ```\n * val instant = Instant.fromEpochSeconds(1709898983, 123456789)\n * instant.toLocalDateTime(TimeZone.of(\"Europe/Berlin\")).date // 2024-03-08\n * ```\n *\n * ### Arithmetic operations\n *\n * #### Elapsed-time-based\n *\n * The [plus] and [minus] operators can be used to add [Duration]s to and subtract them from an [Instant]:\n *\n * ```\n * Clock.System.now() + 5.seconds // 5 seconds from now\n * ```\n *\n * Durations can also be represented as multiples of some [time-based datetime unit][DateTimeUnit.TimeBased]:\n *\n * ```\n * Clock.System.now().plus(4, DateTimeUnit.HOUR) // 4 hours from now\n * ```\n *\n * Also, there is a [minus] operator that returns the [Duration] representing the difference between two instants:\n *\n * ```\n * val start = Clock.System.now()\n * val concertStart = LocalDateTime(2023, 1, 1, 20, 0, 0).toInstant(TimeZone.of(\"Europe/Berlin\"))\n * val timeUntilConcert = concertStart - start\n * ```\n *\n * #### Calendar-based\n *\n * Since [Instant] represents a point in time, it is always well-defined what the result of arithmetic operations on it\n * is, including the cases when a calendar is used.\n * This is not the case for [LocalDateTime], where the result of arithmetic operations depends on the time zone.\n * See the [LocalDateTime] documentation for more details.\n *\n * Adding and subtracting calendar-based units can be done using the [plus] and [minus] operators,\n * requiring a [TimeZone]:\n *\n * ```\n * // One day from now in Berlin\n * Clock.System.now().plus(1, DateTimeUnit.DAY, TimeZone.of(\"Europe/Berlin\"))\n *\n * // A day and two hours short from two months later in Berlin\n * Clock.System.now().plus(DateTimePeriod(months = 2, days = -1, hours = -2), TimeZone.of(\"Europe/Berlin\"))\n * ```\n *\n * The difference between [Instant] values in terms of calendar-based units can be obtained using the [periodUntil]\n * method:\n *\n * ```\n * val start = Clock.System.now()\n * val concertStart = LocalDateTime(2023, 1, 1, 20, 0, 0).toInstant(TimeZone.of(\"Europe/Berlin\"))\n * val timeUntilConcert = start.periodUntil(concertStart, TimeZone.of(\"Europe/Berlin\"))\n * // Two months, three days, four hours, and five minutes until the concert\n * ```\n *\n * Or the [Instant.until] method, as well as [Instant.daysUntil], [Instant.monthsUntil],\n * and [Instant.yearsUntil] extension functions:\n *\n * ```\n * val start = Clock.System.now()\n * val concertStart = LocalDateTime(2023, 1, 1, 20, 0, 0).toInstant(TimeZone.of(\"Europe/Berlin\"))\n * val timeUntilConcert = start.until(concertStart, DateTimeUnit.DAY, TimeZone.of(\"Europe/Berlin\"))\n * // 63 days until the concert, rounded down\n * ```\n *\n * ### Platform specifics\n *\n * On the JVM, there are `Instant.toJavaInstant()` and `java.time.Instant.toKotlinInstant()`\n * extension functions to convert between `kotlinx.datetime` and `java.time` objects used for the same purpose.\n * Similarly, on the Darwin platforms, there are `Instant.toNSDate()` and `NSDate.toKotlinInstant()`\n * extension functions.\n *\n * ### Construction, serialization, and deserialization\n *\n * [fromEpochSeconds] can be used to construct an instant from the number of seconds since\n * `1970-01-01T00:00:00Z` (the Unix epoch).\n * [epochSeconds] and [nanosecondsOfSecond] can be used to obtain the number of seconds and nanoseconds since the epoch.\n *\n * ```\n * val instant = Instant.fromEpochSeconds(1709898983, 123456789)\n * instant.epochSeconds // 1709898983\n * instant.nanosecondsOfSecond // 123456789\n * ```\n *\n * [fromEpochMilliseconds] allows constructing an instant from the number of milliseconds since the epoch.\n * [toEpochMilliseconds] can be used to obtain the number of milliseconds since the epoch.\n * Note that [Instant] supports nanosecond precision, so converting to milliseconds is a lossy operation.\n *\n * ```\n * val instant1 = Instant.fromEpochSeconds(1709898983, 123456789)\n * instant1.nanosecondsOfSecond // 123456789\n * val milliseconds = instant1.toEpochMilliseconds() // 1709898983123\n * val instant2 = Instant.fromEpochMilliseconds(milliseconds)\n * instant2.nanosecondsOfSecond // 123000000\n * ```\n *\n * [parse] and [toString] methods can be used to obtain an [Instant] from and convert it to a string in the\n * ISO 8601 extended format.\n *\n * ```\n * val instant = Instant.parse(\"2023-01-02T22:35:01+01:00\")\n * instant.toString() // 2023-01-02T21:35:01Z\n * ```\n *\n * During parsing, the UTC offset is not returned separately.\n * If the UTC offset is important, use [DateTimeComponents] with [DateTimeComponents.Formats.ISO_DATE_TIME_OFFSET] to\n * parse the string instead.\n *\n * [Instant.parse] and [Instant.format] also accept custom formats:\n *\n * ```\n * val customFormat = DateTimeComponents.Format {\n *   date(LocalDate.Formats.ISO)\n *   char(' ')\n *   time(LocalTime.Formats.ISO)\n *   char(' ')\n *   offset(UtcOffset.Formats.ISO)\n * }\n * val instant = Instant.parse(\"2023-01-02 22:35:01.14 +01:00\", customFormat)\n * instant.format(customFormat, offset = UtcOffset(hours = 2)) // 2023-01-02 23:35:01.14 +02:00\n * ```\n *\n * Additionally, there are several `kotlinx-serialization` serializers for [Instant]:\n * - [InstantIso8601Serializer] for the ISO 8601 extended format.\n * - [InstantComponentSerializer] for an object with components.\n *\n * @see LocalDateTime for a user-visible representation of moments in time in an unspecified time zone.\n */\n@Serializable(with = InstantIso8601Serializer::class)\npublic expect class Instant : Comparable<Instant> {\n\n    /**\n     * The number of seconds from the epoch instant `1970-01-01T00:00:00Z` rounded down to a [Long] number.\n     *\n     * The difference between the rounded number of seconds and the actual number of seconds\n     * is returned by [nanosecondsOfSecond] property expressed in nanoseconds.\n     *\n     * Note that this number doesn't include leap seconds added or removed since the epoch.\n     *\n     * @see fromEpochSeconds\n     * @sample {"path":"core/common/src/format/Unicode.kt","prefix":"/*\n * Copyright 2019-2023 JetBrains s.r.o. and contributors.\n * Use of this source code is governed by the Apache 2.0 License that can be found in the LICENSE.txt file.\n */\n\npackage kotlinx.datetime.format\n\nimport kotlin.native.concurrent.*\n\n/**\n * Marks declarations in the datetime library that use format strings to define datetime formats.\n *\n * Format strings are discouraged, because they require gaining proficiency in another tiny language.\n * When possible, please use the builder-style Kotlin API instead.\n * If the format string is a constant, the corresponding builder-style Kotlin code can be obtained by calling\n * [DateTimeFormat.formatAsKotlinBuilderDsl] on the resulting format. For example:\n * ```\n * DateTimeFormat.formatAsKotlinBuilderDsl(LocalTime.Format { byUnicodePattern(\"HH:mm\") })\n * ```\n */\n@MustBeDocumented\n@Retention(value = AnnotationRetention.BINARY)\n@RequiresOptIn(\n    level = RequiresOptIn.Level.WARNING,\n    message = \"Using format strings is discouraged.\" +\n            \" If the format string is a constant, the corresponding builder-style Kotlin code can be obtained by calling\" +\n            \" `DateTimeFormat.formatAsKotlinBuilderDsl` on the resulting format.\"\n)\npublic annotation class FormatStringsInDatetimeFormats\n\n/**\n * Appends a Unicode datetime format string to the [DateTimeFormatBuilder].\n *\n * This is the format string syntax used by the Java Time's `DateTimeFormatter` class, Swift's and Objective-C's\n * `NSDateFormatter` class, and the ICU library.\n * The syntax is specified at\n * <https://unicode-org.github.io/icu/userguide/format_parse/datetime/#datetime-format-syntax>.\n *\n * Currently, locale-aware directives are not supported, due to no locale support in Kotlin.\n *\n * In addition to the standard syntax, this function also supports the following extensions:\n * * `[]` denote optional sections. For example, `hh:mm[:ss]` will allow parsing seconds optionally.\n *   This is similar to what is supported by the Java Time's `DateTimeFormatter` class.\n *\n * Usage example:\n * ```\n * DateTimeComponents.Format {\n *   // 2023-01-20T23:53:16.312+03:30[Asia/Tehran]\n *   byUnicodePattern(\"uuuu-MM-dd'T'HH:mm[:ss[.SSS]]xxxxx'['VV']'\")\n * }\n * ```\n *\n * The list of supported directives is as follows:\n *\n * | **Directive**       | **Meaning**                                                                             |\n * | ------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |\n * | `'string'`          | literal `string`, without quotes                                                        |\n * | `'''`               | literal char `'`                                                                        |\n * | `[fmt]`             | equivalent to `fmt` during formatting, but during parsing also accepts the empty string |\n * | `u`                 | ISO year without padding                                                                |\n * | `uu`                | last two digits of the ISO year, with the base year 2000                                |\n * | `uuuu`              | ISO year, zero-padded to four digits                                                    |\n * | `M`, `L`            | month number (1-12), without padding                                                    |\n * | `MM`, `LL`          | month number (01-12), zero-padded to two digits                                         |\n * | `d`                 | day-of-month (1-31), without padding                                                    |\n * | `H`                 | hour-of-day (0-23), without padding                                                     |\n * | `HH`                | hour-of-day (00-23), zero-padded to two digits                                          |\n * | `m`                 | minute-of-hour (0-59), without padding                                                  |\n * | `mm`                | minute-of-hour (00-59), zero-padded to two digits                                       |\n * | `s`                 | second-of-hour (0-59), without padding                                                  |\n * | `ss`                | second-of-hour (00-59), zero-padded to two digits                                       |\n * | `S`, `SS`, `SSS`... | fraction-of-second without a leading dot, with as many digits as the format length      |\n * | `VV`                | timezone name (for example, `Europe/Berlin`)                                            |\n *\n * The UTC offset is formatted using one of the following directives. In every one of these formats, hours, minutes,\n * and seconds are zero-padded to two digits. Also, hours are unconditionally present.\n * \n * | **Directive**          | **Minutes** | **Seconds** | **Separator** | **Representation of zero** |\n * | ---------------------- | ----------- | ----------- | ------------- | -------------------------- |\n * | `X`                    | unless zero | never       | none          | `Z`                        |\n * | `XX`                   | always      | never       | none          | `Z`                        |\n * | `XXX`                  | always      | never       | colon         | `Z`                        |\n * | `XXXX`                 | always      | unless zero | none          | `Z`                        |\n * | `XXXXX`, `ZZZZZ`       | always      | unless zero | colon         | `Z`                        |\n * | `x`                    | unless zero | never       | none          | `+00`                      |\n * | `xx`, `Z`, `ZZ`, `ZZZ` | always      | never       | none          | `+0000`                    |\n * | `xxx`                  | always      | never       | colon         | `+00:00`                   |\n * | `xxxx`                 | always      | unless zero | none          | `+0000`                    |\n * | `xxxxx`                | always      | unless zero | colon         | `+00:00`                   |\n *\n * Additionally, because the `y` directive is very often used instead of `u`, they are taken to mean the same.\n * This may lead to unexpected results if the year is negative: `y` would always produce a positive number, whereas\n * `u` may sometimes produce a negative one. For example:\n * ```\n * LocalDate(-10, 1, 5).format { byUnicodeFormat(\"yyyy-MM-dd\") } // -0010-01-05\n * LocalDate(-10, 1, 5).toJavaLocalDate().format(java.time.format.DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern(\"yyyy-MM-dd\")) // 0011-01-05\n * ```\n *\n * Note that, when the format includes the era directive, [byUnicodePattern] will fail with an exception, so almost all\n * of the intentional usages of `y` will correctly report an error instead of behaving slightly differently.\n *\n * @throws IllegalArgumentException if the pattern is invalid or contains unsupported directives.\n * @throws IllegalArgumentException if the builder is incompatible with the specified directives.\n * @throws UnsupportedOperationException if the kotlinx-datetime library does not support the specified directives.\n * @sample kotlinx.datetime.test.samples.format.UnicodeSamples.byUnicodePattern\n */\n@FormatStringsInDatetimeFormats\npublic [instants][Instant], decomposed into date and time components.\n *\n * The date components are: [years] ([DateTimeUnit.YEAR]), [months] ([DateTimeUnit.MONTH]), and [days] ([DateTimeUnit.DAY]).\n *\n * The time components are: [hours] ([DateTimeUnit.HOUR]), [minutes] ([DateTimeUnit.MINUTE]),\n * [seconds] ([DateTimeUnit.SECOND]), and [nanoseconds] ([DateTimeUnit.NANOSECOND]).\n *\n * The time components are not independent and are always normalized together.\n * Likewise, months are normalized together with years.\n * For example, there is no difference between `DateTimePeriod(months = 24, hours = 2, minutes = 63)` and\n * `DateTimePeriod(years = 2, hours = 3, minutes = 3)`.\n *\n * All components can also be negative: for example, `DateTimePeriod(months = -5, days = 6, hours = -3)`.\n * Whereas `months = 5` means \"5 months after,\" `months = -5` means \"5 months earlier.\"\n *\n * A constant time interval that consists of a single non-zero component (like \"yearly\" or \"quarterly\") should be\n * represented by a [DateTimeUnit] directly instead of a [DateTimePeriod]:\n * for example, instead of `DateTimePeriod(months = 6)`, one could use `DateTimeUnit.MONTH * 6`.\n * This provides a wider variety of operations: for example, finding how many such intervals fit between two instants\n * or dates or adding a multiple of such intervals at once.\n *\n * ### Interaction with other entities\n *\n * [DateTimePeriod] can be returned from [Instant.periodUntil], representing the difference between two instants.\n * Conversely, there is an [Instant.plus] overload that accepts a [DateTimePeriod] and returns a new instant.\n *\n * [DatePeriod] is a subtype of [DateTimePeriod] that only stores the date components and has all time components equal\n * to zero.\n *\n * [DateTimePeriod] can be thought of as a combination of a [Duration] and a [DatePeriod], as it contains both the\n * time components of [Duration] and the date components of [DatePeriod].\n * [Duration.toDateTimePeriod] can be used to convert a [Duration] to the corresponding [DateTimePeriod].\n *\n * ### Construction, serialization, and deserialization\n *\n * When a [DateTimePeriod] is constructed in any way, a [DatePeriod] value, which is a subtype of [DateTimePeriod],\n * will be returned if all time components happen to be zero.\n *\n * A `DateTimePeriod` can be constructed using the constructor function with the same name.\n * See sample 1.\n *\n * [parse] and [toString] methods can be used to obtain a [DateTimePeriod] from and convert it to a string in the\n * ISO 8601 extended format.\n * See sample 2.\n *\n * `DateTimePeriod` can also be returned as the result of instant arithmetic operations (see [Instant.periodUntil]).\n *\n * Additionally, there are several `kotlinx-serialization` serializers for [DateTimePeriod]:\n * - [DateTimePeriodIso8601Serializer] for the ISO 8601 format;\n * - [DateTimePeriodComponentSerializer]  for an object
